newsitem.title: USA: Hashimoto sees China cautious on Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Hashimoto sees China cautious on Hong Kong.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto has said he does not expect Beijing to clamp down on Hong Kong after the handover of the British colony set for midnight June 30.

"We do have some concern, of course, but at the same time, I think the Chinese leadership are fully aware that China stands to lose if they try to crush the system that has made possible the prosperity in Hong Kong," Hashimoto told U.S. public television in a remarks taped on Friday and aired on Monday.
Hashimoto, speaking through an interpreter, noted China's size and influence in the region and said Tokyo and Washington should improve their relationships with Beijing.
"Rather than seeing China as an adversary, we should try our best ... to incorporate China as a constructive partner," Hashimoto told the "NewsHour with Jim Lehrer."
This would benefit Japan and the United States and the region as a whole, Hashimoto said.
Japan and the United States are cooperating in a drive for China's participation in the World Trade Organisation.
Citing challenges raised by the handover of Hong Kong to China, Hashimoto said Japan had voiced its concerns to Chinese officials.
Some "specifically said that they have no intention of eliminating the basis for the prosperity of Hong Kong." Other officials "did not seem very pleased," he said.

"I think, in reality the Chinese will be very cautious in their approach towards Hong Kong, because if they are to crush the basis for prosperity for Hong Kong, they will lose major market opportunities," he said.

A poll commissioned by the English-language South China Morning Post and released Monday said 57 percent of respondents expected Hong Kong to be as prosperous in the future as it was now, while 25 percent thought it would become even more prosperous.
Up to 51 percent expected the British colony of more than 150 years to remain stable after it is handed back to China, while 34 percent felt that stability would suffer, the poll showed.
